description: Golden corpus for authorization_decision.v1 (CHAOS-4932). reject_by_client documents VALIDATE against the schema and every client MUST still refuse them.

accept.why: TRD section 8's own decision example, plus redaction, assurance and step-up.
A deny: no obligations, a reason code, an expiry. Positive control for the deny branch.
A platform decision has a null organization_id, as in principal.v1.
An empty allowlist means none; it is representable and distinct from an absent member.
An allow with no obligations is legal.

reject.why: `allowed` has no default. A document with no verdict must not be read as one.
The string "true" is not a boolean; a truthy-string coercion would turn text into an allow.
null is not a verdict.
1 is not a boolean.
Decision expiry bounds a stale allow (TRD section 14); a deny without one is invalid too. Ruled Q2: keep.
The allow case of the same rule, so the requirement is not accidentally deny-only.
policy_revision is in every decision (ACP-ADR-05 decision 3).
A decision states why.
The member is required; null is the explicit platform value, absence is a defect.
Free text smuggled into the code field: user-facing text is caller-owned.
Codes are lowercase tokens.
An obligation the contract does not define fails closed, not ignored.
Redaction classes are closed.
Assurance by reference to principal.v1's closed set.
A string is not a boolean.
A repeated entry.
Canonical lowercase keys only.
A deny that carries obligations.
Server-minted shape.
A timestamp, by reference to principal.v1.
A revision is a non-negative counter.
Not a number.
A decision claiming to be error.v1 (or the reverse) is not a decision.
Closed document.
A lowercase secret-shaped token fits the old shape pattern; the closed vocabulary refuses it.
A well-formed code no producer emits is refused: the vocabulary is closed.

reject_by_client.why: An allow whose expires_at is long past. Valid for the schema (a timestamp is a timestamp); TRD section 14 makes expiry the bound on a stale allow, so a client that hands back allowed=true for it exposes a decision nobody may reuse. Both clients refuse it against a stated `now`.

`allowed` appears twice, false then true. Every parser keeps the last, so the survivor is a well-formed ALLOW that the schema validates; only the raw bytes show the verdict was ambiguous. The client must refuse on the bytes.

42.0 is a valid JSON Schema integer, so all three validators accept it. A float64 reader has already rounded a decimal-form token, so it is indistinguishable from the integer it rounds to; both clients refuse it (wire-integer rule). Valid for the schema, refused by the client.
